content: Now that there is a dedicated channel, maybe we should agree on a definition (or one exists I am not aware, apologies). Is autoformalization - "AI writes Lean and I mostly don't read it or touch it" (i.e. what is vibecoding in traditional software these days) or more widely "AI was used to write Lean" (which would include what would be AI-assisted development in traditional coding) or maybe specifically only translating existing informal math?
Just saw the channel title too, maybe the size of the artifact is what make it "autoformalization"?
Autoformalization is about converting PDFs to Lean, which isn't the same as vibe proving

Traditionally, autoformalization has meant machine conversion of an existing proof, written in natural language, into a formal proof. The contrast is with automated theorem proving, which means finding a proof of a conjecture, or proving new theorems. That is, the distinction is whether the proof is already known and written down informally, or whether the proof is unknown.

The distinction was perhaps clearer back in the days when automated theorem proving mostly meant running a relatively simple algorithm like resolution, which was a very different task from natural language processing. In today's world, the lines have blurred.

In the early days of AI for theorem proving, the main goal of autoformalization was to formalize statements, not proofs. Also at the time, systems were more specific in their tasks, so people trained prover and autoformalizers separately. One of the first major results to show traction on this problem was Autoformalization with Large Language Models using Codex (pre-chat GPT) showing a 25.3% success rate in formalizing statements. Autoformalizing statements (and definitions) is still really important. It doesn't matter if the proof is exactly the same as the paper as long as it passes Lean, but if the definitions or theorems are different, then that is an issue, and not one that is easy to automatically verify, so that is why it is still a topic of interest apart from formalization of proofs.

Of course, formalization of proofs was always part of the main goal, including in the paper A Promising Path Towards Autoformalization and General Artificial Intelligence (which might have been the work that coined this term). And just after Autoformalization with Large Language Models was Draft, Sketch, and Prove, which formalized proofs (both human written and AI-generated) into formal sketches which were filled in by an automated theorem prover.

Now the situation is complicated. General purpose models like Leanstral happily do it all (and can do it autonomously or with human feedback). The recent https://www.math.inc/formalqualbench "autoformalization" benchmark has no natural language proofs. Instead, it is just understood that these are well-known theorems and either the model has memorized the proof or can use the internet to look it up. But interestingly, as agents get more powerful, this even started to address the autoformalization of lemmas/definitions, since the model can use the success of the full large proof as a way to check the correctness of whether it translated an intermediate lemma/definition correctly.

So in summary:

  • Autoformalization of proofs is quickly getting confused with automatic theorem proving (ATP) and with vibe proving. The only (small) distinction is that for the former, there is an existing proof available to consult (maybe just in the model's memory), and for the latter, there could be a human in the loop.
  • Autoformalization of definitions and statements is still interesting in its own right because it is hard to check for correctness.

In my mind the meaning of the word right now is about taking large informal language corpora, e.g. articles and textbooks, and trying to produce a corresponding formal artefact "automatically". In practice today, "automatically" mostly means some combination of prompting and orchestrating LLMs, perhaps which have been RL'd on Lean. In particular, a lot of the difficulty is about correctly translating definitions, not just translating proofs, and maintaining coherence / sensible behaviour across article or book scale projects, where you will have to build deep chains of dependencies away from what is available in Mathlib.

I wish we could somehow maintain a distinction between translating natural language into formal language (autoformalization) and auto-complete of proof statements, but it seems like that ship is quickly sailing. I’m not familiar with contemporary approaches that only autoformalize statements without integrating proof completion. To me, arriving at a good formal definition or theorem statement is a question of semantics, while proving a formal theorem statement to be true or false is a question of syntax, and that gulf is wide enough that it would be nice to have separate terms for those.

I think there's some hope that "autoformalization" will retain its connotation of "natural language -> formal language." But I would expect the word to cover natural language definitions and natural language theorem statements and natural language proofs, rather than being restricted to only one or the other.

Unfortunately for those of us who want to maintain clear distinctions, "natural language -> formal language" does not by itself preclude "human prompt -> Lean code" (i.e., vibe coding in Lean), which is quite a different activity from converting a traditional journal article or book into Lean. So we're probably going to have to live with different people using the word to mean different things.
From a talk by Auguste Poiroux (#Event announcements > Hybrid talks on Lean, AI, and sphere packing @ 💬):

thank you all for replies, sounds like there is a rich history of "autoformalization", but the arrival of current generation much more capable AI's has muddied the water a bit:

Unfortunately for those of us who want to maintain clear distinctions, "natural language -> formal language"

The broadest definition is:

1) the mathematical content is not novel - otherwise it will be autoproving
2) the input is natural language
3) the output is formal proof

and since current AIs do input natural language - be it human rigorous proof or less than rigorous proof sketch, and similarly can take a narrow instruction "formalize this internal proof step", or very wide "formalize this book" - they oblige, thus "autoformalization" likely to used in the broadest sense, while some subcategories start to emerge. I have heard people use "semi-autoformalization" to capture a more granular workflows where the human steers more.

Maybe also worth noting that the word "novel" is also a bit murky. If a result has a known natural-language proof but the AI comes up with the proof independently, then in some sense the proof is not "novel"; but the AI is in effect autoproving. Even more confusingly, it's not crazy to describe what a tactic such as "grind" is doing as "autoproving," even though we almost certainly don't want to call that "novel."

That said, I think what you say about the term "autoformalization" is sensible.

yeah, makes sense, also practically these days "the AI comes up with the proof independently" is hard to prove since model are trained on all of the internet.

(aside) I read somewhere that Kuhn had a very specific definition (in philosophy of science) for "paradigm shift", but then his book "Structure Of Scientific Revolutions" became popular and people just started to use "paradigm shift" in any context and word lost its tighter original definition.

It’s perhaps unwise for me to re-ignite the discussion when I don’t really expect to have the time to properly participate, but I’m beginning to think it is worth distinguishing between verification and formalisation. I think there is now ample evidence to say that frontier models have the capability to autoverify complex mathematical proofs. Is there as much to say they are good at autoformalising them? Especially at scale?

It is not a distinction I know how to make concretely, in that there is a subjectivity to the question of “what really makes a formalisation”. It’s something I’ve been thinking about for quite some time, and it’s not a question I have nearly enough expertise or experience to even begin to try and answer, but it is a question I think is actively being posed in some form or another, far beyond this thread. I don’t think it is an easy question to answer, but I also think that each time something new is merged to Mathlib, or any big downstream project, in some implicit way, it is.

There is often a great deal of discussion around “autoformalisation” efforts, and I wonder if the friction we sometimes see in these discussions stems from the (possibly completely unintentional) conflation of the two terms. I think that both verification and formalisation are valuable, but serve different purposes (complementary, related, but different). I also think that it would be nice if autoverifications start converging towards autoformalisation.

Anyway, to end the ramble, I think I’m personally going to start distinguishing the two and using the term “autoverification” to describe “autonomously generated sorry-free proofs” and the term “autoformalisation” to describe “autoverifications that sufficiently well-organised, general, modular, broad, robust, readable, and otherwise compliant with the general standards of this community”.

I like the distinction you're trying to draw, but the terms "autoverification" and "autoformalization" are so similar to each other that I think people will find them confusing. If you insist on a single word, perhaps you could consider a neologism, such as "autolibrarization" for what you're calling "autoformalization" (i.e., autonomously writing code with high enough quality to be incorporated into a standard library).

I honestly think that distinguishing between those two terms is not much more than shifting goalposts.

Even a year ago, if some of the recent big AI formalisation had been done by hand, would have been celebrated as a big success, no matter the code quality or if the API is usable outside etc.

Of course a mathlib style (reusable, fast, ...) formalisation is far better (and harder), but for the vast majority of people, I dont think they will care too much about that, especially when using formalisation as a tool in verifying LLM output / math proofs.

If FLT will be finished by some AI in a few months in a completely unusable way, that would be reported on and not if it was finished in a tidy way a few minths later.

Additionally, I feel like LLM Lean code of general purpose models (funnily enough not by specialized autoformalisation AI tools) has gotten far better. Except for the length of proofs and code comments, it has become very difficult for me to judge whether some mathlib PR is by a human or Claude code.

I feel there always has been a bit of murkiness around the ultimate vision for formalized math, but since formalization was so laborious for humans and niche in math community that wasn't a problem until AI arrived and made formalization at scale actually feasible.

So the "auto-" part of the "autoverification" vs "autoformalization" is not needed, the real question is "why formalize?":
1) pure verification (no human needed apart from confirming the challenge.lean)
2) deeper human understanding and all the other activities listed here https://www.imo.universite-paris-saclay.fr/~patrick.massot/files/exposition/why_formalize.pdf.

autoverifications that sufficiently well-organised, general, modular, broad, robust, readable, and otherwise compliant with the general standards of this community”.

All of these distinctions will disappear very soon (if not already). I don't see a very compelling reason to believe that AI can't write readable, modular proofs. I know that some previous attempts didn't, but AI capabilities have improved greatly since then, and will continue to improve.

The one distinction that will always remain there will be two types of formalizations (both done with AI, because soon it will be foolish not use it in some capacity):

  • formalization for verification - a human has not looked at the lean code, at most read the challenge.lean used at the final comparator run.
  • formalization for understanding - a human has also read, understood and maybe directed the formalization on finer lever - modules, theorems, down to tactics.

but note these cannot be detected from the github repo alone.
actually worried about AI written definition, which could be poisonous if later user only check their theorem statement

I think defining autoformalization as moving from natural language to formal language is complicated by the fact that essentially all math writing already contains tons of “formal” language. Math papers are full of mathematical syntax (why LaTeX is a necessity) that would hardly be considered NL. A lot of this syntax is quite sophisticated and even comes with its own rules of syntactic manipulation. For instance, algebraic equations like “x+3=5” quite clearly adhere to a rigid syntax and are manipulated syntactically during the proving process. I think a lot of this mathematical syntax is just so ubiquitous that we don’t often think about it as a mini version of formalization. After all, I could (with some difficulty) express the same idea without the syntax: “the result of adding some integer to the value three is equal to the value 5.” Historically math statement were expressed in this way.

Now, we could just define natural language as “anything that isn’t a formal language with a rigid grammar,” but I think this is somewhat of a sweeping generalization, since informal math statements can have vastly different levels of formalization and abstraction. For instance, suppose we task an LLM with autoformalizing the following two statements into Lean:

  1. Johnny starts with an unspecified number of apples. He gets three more, and now he has five apples. This must mean that Johnny started with two apples
  2. (x+3=5)—>x=2, where x is some integer

You can imagine tons of slightly different ways of autoformalzing the first statement to capture the same logical meaning. But an LLM would likely have to abstract away a lot of unnecessary info either way. But for the second statement, there really isn’t any abstraction that needs to be done. This is really more of an “auto-translation” problem from one formal language to another. This strikes me as a completely separate skill, and likely both auto-abstraction and auto-translation are involved in the autoformalization process.

On this Zulip, "informal" means "text written in a natural language such as English", however formal it may be, and "formal" means "code written in Lean". We're aware that it does not conform to the usual English usage of these words.
I think the “however formal it may be” part hides a lot of nuance that could be relevant for the task of autoformalization
Namely, autoformalizing a highly informal NL statement might require different skills than autoformalizing a highly formal NL statement

At the extreme, if a text is so formal that it almost entirely adheres to some other rigid grammar that isn’t Lean’s, then autoformalization is essentially just a translation task. Completely different than the more general task of autoformalization.
